phonemes.desc: Aspirated rho [rʰ], the breathy initial consonant preserved in the rough breathing.
Short epsilon with acute [é], the pitch peak of the name.
Long alpha [aː], the feminine ending that gives the name its dignity.

pronunciation.approximation: 'RHAY-ah' — begin with a breathy 'r', stress the middle syllable, and draw out the final 'ah'.

kin.label: Greek
kin.form: Ῥέα (Rhéā), Titaness — possibly connected to ῥέω (rhéō), 'to flow', though the etymology is uncertain (Beekes)

kin.label: Epic
kin.form: Ῥείη (Rheiē) — the Homeric/Hesiodic form of the name, with the same meaning and dignity

kin.label: Anatolian
kin.form: Compared by ancient and modern scholars with the Phrygian Mother of the Gods; the Greeks themselves made the identification (Pausanias 7.17)

pronunciation.note: Rhéā is Tier 1 because the restoration preserves both the acute stress on the second syllable and the long final alpha (Ῥέᾱ) — two distinctive features that plain ASCII 'Rhea' loses. She is the great mother of the Olympian generation.

domains.title: Mother of the Gods
domains.subtitle: Fertility, Mountain, Maternal Cunning
domains.lead: Rhéā is the Titaness who gave birth to the Olympian gods and saved the youngest, Zeus, from being swallowed by his father Kronos. She is the mountain mother, the fertile earth, and the cunning protector of divine succession — the hinge between the old gods and the new.

cards.name: Mother of Olympians
cards.desc: By Kronos she bore Hestia, Demeter, Hera, Hades, Poseidon, and Zeus — the entire next divine generation.

cards.name: Protector of Zeus
cards.desc: She hid the infant Zeus in a Cretan cave and gave Kronos a stone in swaddling clothes — the first trick in Greek mythology.

cards.name: Mountain Goddess
cards.desc: Worshipped on Crete's peaks and in Phrygia; the Greeks identified her with the wild Mother of the mountains.

cards.name: Fertility and Flow
cards.desc: Her possible link to rhéō, 'to flow', ties her to springs, milk, and the unceasing abundance of the living earth.

symbols.name: Swaddled stone (Omphalos)
symbols.meaning: The great stone she wrapped in infant's clothes and gave to Kronos; it was later displayed at Delphi as the navel of the world (Pausanias 10.16.3)

symbols.name: Cretan cave
symbols.meaning: The hiding place of the infant Zeus — the sources disagree between Mount Ida and Mount Dikte, and both caves became cult sites

symbols.name: Lion
symbols.meaning: The mountain beast of her later iconography, borrowed from the Phrygian Mother — Rhéā's lions are Cybele's lions

symbols.name: Tympanon drum
symbols.meaning: The frame drum of ecstatic mountain cult; in the myth it is the beat that once hid the infant's cries from his father

mythology.lead: Rhéā's myth is the hinge between Titanic and Olympian rule. She endures Kronos's violence, then engineers the survival of the son who will overthrow him — the story of how the Olympians were born twice: once in her womb, and once out of a trick.

myths.title: The Devoured Five
myths.text: Rhéā's marriage was a maternity under siege. Wedded to her brother Kronos, she bore him Hestía, Deméter, Hēra, Hádēs, and Poseidôn — and each infant, ‘as soon as each was born from the holy womb’, Kronos gulped down whole, for he had learned from Gaia and starry Ouranós that it was fated for him to be overthrown by his own son, though he was mighty, and he kept ever watchful, waiting for it (Theogony 453–467). Rhéā's grief is one of the quietest devastations in Greek poetry — Hesiod records no cry, no protest, only the fact that she bore children into a father who was also a mouth. The myth means that her story begins in the oldest nightmare of motherhood: the body that nourishes and the body that consumes are the same. Her later cunning is forged in this silence.

myths.title: The Stone in Swaddling Clothes
myths.text: When Rhéā was pregnant with Zeus, she finally turned from grieving mother to strategist. She went to her own parents, Gaia and Ouranós, and they sent her to Crete, to Lyktos, where she bore the great Zeus in a hidden cave — ‘in the land of Crete, in a rich and secret place’ (Theogony 468–474). Gaia took the child into her arms and hid him in a cave deep within the divine earth, in the dense woods of Mount Aigaion; Rhéā meanwhile wrapped a great stone in swaddling bands and gave it to Kronos, who took it in his hands and gulped it down, the fool, not knowing that the stone, instead of a son, lay in his stone-like belly (Theogony 475–491). Later tradition displayed the stone at Delphi, where Pausanias saw it, anointed with oil (10.16.3). The myth means that the world's navel began as a decoy: the center of the cosmos was once a mother's lie, and it saved everything.

myths.title: The Kouretes' Clashing Shield
myths.text: A god hidden in a cave is a god whose cry must be masked — and Rhéā's Cretan attendants turned concealment into cult. Callimachus, in his Hymn to Zeus (42–53), imagines the infant's dangerous noise and the remedy: ‘for if you were to see the pipe and the puffed-out dance of the Kouretes... you would say: “The war-gear of the Kouretes is the invention of war-mad Ares; no, Rhea bore you, goddess of many names, she bore you, lion-mouthed”’ — the Curetes beat their shields and stamped their dancing feet so that the child's wailing would not reach his father. Diodorus (5.70) preserves the Cretan tradition that Rhea entrusted the babe to these armed guardians. The cave itself the sources cannot agree on — Ida or Dikte — and the disagreement fed rival Cretan sanctities for centuries. The myth means that the birth of Zeus is also the birth of ritual: the clashing shield, the ecstatic dance, the mystery that hides the god by noise — Cretan religion claimed to reenact the rescue of heaven's king every time it danced.

myths.title: The Mountain Mother of Dionysus
myths.text: In later, Orphic-flavored tradition Rhéā's maternity extends to the other twice-born god. Diodorus (3.73), reporting the Orphic account, tells that after the Titans' attack on the infant Dionysos — the first death of the god — the child was restored, and the rites that surrounded him were those of the Mother: the tympanon, the cymbal, the ecstatic dance, the lion-drawn chariot. Nonnus, in the Dionysiaca (9), has Rhea receive the newborn Dionysos into her wild mountain company, nursing him among the nymphs of the forests. The Greeks had long since identified their Rhéā with the Phrygian Mother of the Gods — Pausanias (7.17) treats the Mother's myth as Rhea's own — so the fosterage of Dionysos by the mountain mother closes a circle: the goddess who saved Zeus from a father also shelters Dionysos from the Titans. The myth means that Rhéā's role outlived the Titanomachy: she is the permanent refuge of the young god against the devouring old order.

lore.syncretism: Rhéā's ancient fate was to be absorbed. The Greeks early identified her with the Phrygian Mother of the Gods — Pausanias (7.17) tells the Mother's myth as Rhea's — and by the classical period the identification was so complete that her name and Cybele's could be interchanged in poetry and cult; the lion, the tympanon, and the mural crown of the Phrygian goddess became Rhea's attributes in Hellenistic and Roman art. The Romans received her as Ops, old Italian goddess of abundance and the stored harvest, consort of Saturn: the Saturnalia's licensed feasting and the Opalia's grain-rites both belong to the complex. Later Neoplatonists read her as the prolific 'source of sources', the middle principle between the hidden father and the manifest gods. Her diffusion is so thorough that 'Rhea' rarely names a distinct theology — which is, in a way, her triumph: the mother of the gods became every mother.
lore.culturalLegacy: Rhéā is the mother without whom there is no Olympus; every Olympian god is her descendant, and her rescue of Zeus is the single act that made the classical pantheon possible. Her myth remains a powerful story of maternal resistance against patriarchal violence — retold by feminist writers as the prototype of the mother who outwits the devouring father. In the heavens she is the second-largest moon of Saturn, discovered by Cassini in 1672, orbiting the planet that bears her consort's Roman name — the couple still paired in the sky. Her name surfaces in fantasy and science fiction as an archetype of primordial motherhood, and in psychology the 'Great Mother' of Jung and Neumann descends in part from her Titaness form. The restoration of Rhéā with its long final alpha restores the drawn-out, dignified cry of the mother of gods.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Rhéā is the mother who learns to deceive in order to protect. She does not confront Kronos directly; she outwits him with a stone. This is not weakness but strategic love — the recognition that survival sometimes requires cunning rather than force.

Her story also holds grief. She bore children only to lose them to her husband's belly. The stone she substitutes is a monument to what was swallowed: time, memory, innocence. When it is vomited up and displayed at Delphi, it becomes the center of the world. Rhea teaches that the things hidden in darkness can become, in time, the axis of a new order.
lore.archaeology: Rhéā's Cretan cult is anchored in two great caves. The Idaean Cave (Ideon Andron) on Mount Ida produced Bronze Age and Archaic votive deposits — bronze shields and vessels, jewelry, and the celebrated inscribed bronze tympanon — showing centuries of continued worship. The Diktean Cave above Psychro, excavated by Hogarth at the end of the nineteenth century, yielded a rich Minoan sanctuary with votive double axes and figurines. Both caves were claimed as Zeus's birthplace, reflecting the Ida/Dikte disagreement preserved in the sources. On the mainland her archaeological footprint merges with that of the Great Mother and of Demeter, a conflation the ancient record itself performs.
